column3: It repeats the focus's test almost verbatim: the final home belongs to one side, while wrongdoers do not prosper.
Revelation arriving from God gives a broad source for the guidance named in the focus.
It joins clear proofs with God's refusal to guide wrongdoing people, clarifying the focus's final judgment on wrongdoers.
Musa calls the arriving truth truth and denies lasting success to its false magical rival.
The immediate later response to truth from God reprises the rejection of Musa's gift and exposes its inconsistency.
It gives righteous action as a general positive route to prospering.
It directly states that the Lord knows both those who stray and those rightly guided.
Their heedlessness adds no distinct account of divine guidance, final outcome, or prosperity.
Guidance and good news for believers offer only a brief general counterpart.
It repeats the Lord's knowledge of guided and straying people after the more direct earlier statement.
Musa's request for a level path supplies early narrative context for his later claim about divine guidance.
Its successful community promotes good and restrains wrong, but does not address the focus's source-and-outcome test.
It applies the focus's rule that wrongdoers do not prosper to a concrete moral refusal.
The sign in Mary and her son does not clarify the focus's claim.
It connects divine guidance and misguidance with observing the final outcome of deniers.
It is a near-verbatim intra-surah parallel: the Lord knows who brought guidance and who is plainly astray.
This scene only precedes Musa's call and does not yet develop guidance or outcome.
It identifies the good final home as the result of enduring faithful conduct.
It repeats that wrongdoers do not prosper and specifies fabrication or denial of God's signs as wrongdoing.
Following unpaying guided messengers offers a general response to the focus's question of who bears guidance.
Seeking God's means and striving supplies a broad positive account of prospering.
It gives non-prospering unbelief as a related but less specific negative judgment.
The employment-marriage agreement does not clarify the focus's criterion of guidance or final outcome.
It adds that inventing lies about God cannot produce prosperity.
It closely parallels the question of who will possess the final home while placing knowledge of all earning with God.
The demand for the promised time adds no account of the focus's guidance or outcome.
God's not guiding defiantly disobedient people is a general counterpart already established more directly.
Musa's signs to Pharaoh's elite, their wrongdoing, and the end of corrupters frame the focus's immediate confrontation.
It assigns guidance and knowledge of the guided to God, in the same surah and close conceptual form.
It presents faithful striving and good things as a positive instance of prospering.
Wrongdoers' dismissal of a messenger as bewitched broadly resembles the rejection around Musa.
The statement about a lineage does not add to the focus.
God's better reward and better outcome give a broad final-outcome counterpart.
It similarly leaves the judgment of the more rightly guided path to the Lord's fuller knowledge.
It identifies Pharaoh, Haman, and their forces as erring, supplying background to the focus's opposition.
Its dwelling and prosperity concern a different communal virtue and add little after the direct outcome cards.
This warning to Nuh does not illuminate Musa's claim about guidance or final outcome.
The reciprocal plotting statement is too general to clarify the focus.
It identifies the final home and its outcome with those who neither seek earthly elevation nor corruption.
Divine knowledge of who is in a doomed town only distantly echoes the focus's knowledge claim.
Musa's encounter at Midian does not develop the focus's issue.
It notes that some received guidance while many became defiant, but without the focus's decisive outcome.
Lut's faith and migration offer a limited example of responding to a prophetic call.
The loss of self and household supplies a broad contrary final outcome.
The true scale and successful heavy balances give a concrete evaluative frame for lasting prosperity.
Submission with excellence is tied to the final outcome of all matters, supporting the focus's outcome criterion.
The nursing episode adds no guidance or outcome claim.
It gives a general moral route to prospering through obedience and freedom from miserliness.
The courtier's act and gratitude test do not materially clarify the focus after earlier guidance cards.
The question to the Samiri supplies no relevant account by itself.
It contrasts faith unmingled with wrongdoing with security and being rightly guided.
The Lord's greater knowledge of all beings is only a distant parallel to knowing the guided.
The warning about Adam's enemy does not clarify the focus's test of guidance.
Musa's confidence that his Lord will guide him supplies a direct narrative counterpart from another Musa scene.
It explicitly names the excellent final home as the fruit of patience.
God's complete dominion over destruction offers only an indirect constraint on wrongdoers' imagined success.
Clear signs and God's guidance by will give a general source-of-guidance parallel.
It calls attention to the final outcome of warned peoples, reinforcing the focus's retrospective test.
The creation statement does not clarify guidance, wrongdoing, or outcome.
It displays a plot's final outcome as the collective destruction of its makers and their people.
The queen's test explicitly asks whether she will be guided or remain unguided.
The disbelievers' inescapable final abode is a general negative outcome already well represented.
The distinction between corrupt and good, despite numbers, broadly supports judging beyond appearances.
A speaker's claim to know from God is a loose narrative echo without the focus's guidance-and-outcome judgment.
Its covenant conditions contrast belief in messengers with departing from the level way.
Pharaoh claims exclusive authority to show the right way, directly contrasting Musa's attribution of guidance to God.
A believer within Pharaoh's household invokes Musa's proofs from the Lord and warns of the promised consequence.
Its prohibition of transgression and command to cooperate in piety give only a broad ethical counterpart.
The Quran's guidance to the most upright course and promise of reward support the focus's truth-and-outcome standard.
It explicitly describes God's messenger as sent with guidance and the religion of truth.
The question to the messengers does not clarify the focus.
It makes the end of powerful sinful predecessors visible evidence that strength cannot secure the final outcome.
The angels' unwearied worship does not develop the focus's claim.
The rhetorical question about daughters and sons is unrelated.
It specifies how God guides followers of His pleasure from darkness to light and to a straight path.
It repeats the prior messenger-with-guidance formulation with little additional marginal value.
Believers' hearing and obedience to God's and the messenger's judgment are identified as prospering.
Purification as prosperity offers a concise but general positive outcome.
The isolated statement about unrepaid favor does not clarify the focus.
Repeated trials without repentance give a general pattern of ignored warning.
It describes believers likely to be guided, but adds little to the already established guidance criterion.
This Musa-and-magicians scene is contextual but adds little after the direct truth-versus-magic card.
Blocking God's path and illicit accumulation give a broad example of conduct opposed to guidance.
The magicians define success as present dominance, providing a false criterion against the focus's lasting outcome.
Musa's request to see his Lord does not clarify the focus's public guidance claim.
Its description of unbelievers adds no distinct route after the stronger wrongdoing judgments.
The immediate continuation identifies following desire without God's guidance as misguidance and says God does not guide wrongdoers.
The exclusive claim to the final home offers only a distant comparison to who truly receives it.
God's refusal to wrong even an atom supports the justice of the focus's judgment on wrongdoers.
It reserves the final outcome of affairs to God while describing righteous use of earthly authority.
The command to worship and persevere does not add to the focus's guidance criterion.
A believer among Pharaoh's people calls them to follow him so he may guide them to the right course.
The expectation of separation supplies no relevant guidance or outcome account.
It joins messengers' clear proofs, the end of prior powerful peoples, and their self-wronging.
Trust in God after turning away does not clarify the focus's test.
It gives the final punishment of wrongdoers as the outcome of an evil alliance.
The bare description of hypocritical speech does not add to the focus.
It states that following God's guidance prevents both straying and misery.
The call to work for such a result offers only a general outcome-oriented exhortation.
Clear signs and God's guidance to a straight path provide a concise closing parallel.
The preceding verse records the rejection of Musa's clear signs as invented magic, setting up his reply in the focus.
Pharaoh's exclusive claim to divinity directly opposes Musa's attribution of guidance and final judgment to the Lord.
It identifies Pharaoh and his hosts' arrogant, unjust assumption that they would not return to God.
The seizure and casting away of Pharaoh and his hosts gives the realized outcome denied by their power.
It states their lasting curse and disgrace, completing the focus's warning about the final home and failed wrongdoing.
The immediate challenge to produce a scripture more guiding than the two revelations clarifies the standard of genuine guidance.
It introduces Musa and Harun's signs to Pharaoh and his elite, directly supplying the contested setting of the focus.
Pharaoh's drowning and belated profession of faith show that coercive recognition cannot reverse the final outcome.
Pharaoh's preserved body is made a sign for later people, extending his outcome into public evidence.
The drowning of Pharaoh's people after their rejection of the signs gives the concrete outcome of their wrongdoing.
Musa tells Pharaoh that the signs came from the Lord and judges Pharaoh bound for destruction.
The command to go to Pharaoh because he has transgressed identifies the wrongdoer confronted by Musa's guidance.
It contrasts peace for whoever follows guidance with punishment for whoever denies and turns away.
Musa's staff-sign before Pharaoh supplies a direct instance of the evidentiary guidance the focus defends.
Musa's confrontation with the gathered magicians forms the immediate truth-versus-magic setting echoed by the focus.
The magicians' faith in the Lord of Musa and Harun shows recognition of the true source of the sign.
The sea's division for Musa and drowning of the opposing group visibly resolves the two competing courses.
It explicitly recounts Musa's coming to Pharaoh, Haman, and Qarun with signs and clear authority.
The believing man contrasts his call to salvation with Pharaoh's party calling toward the Fire.
God protects the believer and surrounds Pharaoh's people with the evil consequence of their plotting.
The Fire appointed for Pharaoh's people supplies the enduring final outcome of their rejection.
It introduces Musa's dispatch with signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, preserving the focus's contested audience.
Pharaoh's boast of earthly dominion displays the temporal power that the focus refuses as a measure of true success.
The drowning of Pharaoh's people gives their collective outcome after they provoked the divine judgment.
The commission to go to Pharaoh because he has transgressed names the wrongdoing behind the focus's verdict.
Pharaoh's claim to be the highest lord directly contests the Lord-centered authority asserted by Musa.
God's exemplary punishment of Pharaoh gives a concise final-outcome confirmation.
